chapters.title: A vision of the Lord’s glory

parts.text: Among the captives beside the river Chebar, Ezekiel sees a storm cloud, fire, and four living creatures. Each has four faces and four wings, and they move wherever the spirit directs them. Their appearance includes human, lion, ox, and eagle features, with brightness like burning coals and movement like lightning.

Beside the creatures are wheels intersecting wheels, with rims full of eyes, moving together with them. Above their heads is an expanse like crystal, and above it a throne with a figure resembling a man. Fire and rainbow-like brightness surround the figure. Ezekiel identifies the vision as the likeness of the LORD’s glory, falls on his face, and hears a voice.

The Spirit sets Ezekiel on his feet, and the Lord sends him to the children of Israel. They and their fathers have rebelled against God, but Ezekiel must deliver the Lord’s words. Whether they listen or refuse, they will know that a prophet has been among them.

Ezekiel is told not to fear their words or hostile looks, even though his situation is compared to living among thorns and scorpions. He must not share their rebellion but receive what God gives him. A hand presents a scroll written on both sides. Its contents are lamentation, mourning, and woe.

chapters.title: The prophet’s duty as a watchman

parts.text: Ezekiel eats the scroll, which tastes sweet as honey, and is sent to Israel with God’s words. Their difficulty is hardness of heart rather than an unfamiliar language. God strengthens Ezekiel to face them without fear. The Spirit carries him to the captives at Tel-abib, where he sits astonished for seven days.

The Lord appoints Ezekiel as a watchman responsible for warning both wicked people and those who turn from righteousness. His duty is to speak faithfully, regardless of their response; failure to warn brings responsibility for their blood. Ezekiel again sees God’s glory in the plain. He is then confined and made unable to speak, except when God opens his mouth to deliver a message.

Ezekiel is commanded to portray Jerusalem on a tile and arrange a model siege around it. An iron pan stands between him and the city. He must lie on his left side for 390 days for Israel’s iniquity and on his right for forty days for Judah’s, with each day explicitly representing a year.

His measured food and water depict the shortages of a besieged city. Bread prepared under defiling conditions represents Israel’s food among the nations. When Ezekiel objects that he has never eaten polluted food, God permits cow dung instead of human dung as fuel. Jerusalem’s inhabitants will eat and drink anxiously as their supplies fail and they waste away because of their iniquity.

chapters.title: The divided hair and Jerusalem’s judgment

parts.text: Ezekiel must shave his head and beard and divide the hair into portions to burn, strike with a sword, and scatter. A few hairs are preserved, though some of these are also burned. God identifies Jerusalem as the subject of the sign: despite her position among the nations, she has rejected his judgments and statutes.

The portions represent death by famine and pestilence, death by the sword, and scattering among the nations. The city’s defilement of God’s sanctuary brings severe judgment, including desperate famine and disgrace before surrounding peoples. The Lord repeatedly declares that he has spoken and will accomplish his anger. Jerusalem’s fate will become both an astonishment and a warning to others.

Ezekiel prophesies against Israel’s mountains, hills, valleys, and rivers, where idolatrous worship has flourished. The Lord will bring the sword, break the images, destroy the altars, and leave bodies before the idols. Cities and high places will become desolate, demonstrating that he is the LORD.

A remnant will escape among the nations. There they will remember the God they abandoned and loathe their own idolatry and evil practices. Yet the coming judgment remains severe: sword, famine, and pestilence will reach those near and far. The places once fragrant with offerings to idols will be marked by death, and the land will be laid waste.

The Lord announces that the end has arrived for the land of Israel. Judgment will answer the people’s own ways and abominations; neither delay nor pity will prevent it. Violence and pride have ripened, and ordinary buying and selling offer no reason for confidence because wrath concerns the whole community.

Although a trumpet calls people to battle, they cannot resist the disaster. Sword, famine, and pestilence bring fear and mourning. Silver and gold cannot rescue or feed them, and the sanctuary’s treasures pass to strangers. Because the land is full of bloodshed, invading nations will possess its houses. Prophets, priests, elders, and rulers will have no effective answer as God judges the people.

While Judah’s elders sit before Ezekiel, the Spirit carries him in a vision to Jerusalem. He sees an image provoking jealousy near the temple entrance. After digging through a wall, he enters a chamber covered with images of creatures and idols. Seventy elders offer incense there, claiming that the Lord does not see them.

Further scenes reveal women mourning for Tammuz and men facing east to worship the sun with their backs toward the LORD’s temple. These practices accompany violence throughout the land. God asks whether such provocations are a small matter and declares that he will act in fury. Their loud cries will not avert the judgment they have brought upon themselves.

In Ezekiel’s vision, armed executioners approach Jerusalem, accompanied by a man clothed in linen with a writing instrument. The LORD commands this man to mark the foreheads of those who grieve over the city’s abominations. The others must follow through the city, sparing those with the mark and beginning judgment at the sanctuary.

As people are struck down, Ezekiel falls on his face and asks whether the whole remnant of Israel will be destroyed. God answers that the land is filled with blood and the city with perverseness; the people claim he has abandoned the earth and does not see. He will repay their conduct. The man in linen reports that he has completed his task.

chapters.title: Glory departs from the temple threshold

parts.text: Ezekiel sees the throne above the cherubims, and the man clothed in linen is instructed to take burning coals from among them and scatter them over Jerusalem. As the LORD’s glory moves to the temple threshold, the house fills with cloud and the court shines with brightness. A cherub gives the man the coals.

The prophet again describes the wheels, their coordinated movement, and the eyes covering the creatures and wheels. He recognizes these beings as the cherubims he saw by the river Chebar. The LORD’s glory leaves the threshold and stands above them. They rise and move to the east gate of the LORD’s house, with God’s glory still above them.

chapters.title: Judgment and a promised new heart

parts.text: At Jerusalem’s east gate, Ezekiel is shown leaders who give wicked counsel and claim security within the city. God knows their thoughts and charges them with filling the streets with the slain. They will be brought out and judged rather than protected by Jerusalem. When Pelatiah dies as Ezekiel prophesies, the prophet cries out for Israel’s remnant.

God answers those who dismiss the exiles by promising to be their sanctuary abroad and gather them back to Israel. He will give them one heart and a new spirit, replacing their stony heart so they may obey him. Those devoted to abominations still face judgment. God’s glory moves to the mountain east of the city, and Ezekiel returns in vision to report to the captives.

chapters.title: The sign of an exile’s baggage

parts.text: Ezekiel packs belongings for exile, digs through a wall, and carries his load out at dusk with his face covered. God explains that this sign concerns Jerusalem’s prince and people. The prince will be caught and taken to Babylon, though he will not see it. His supporters will scatter, while a few survivors will testify among the nations.

Ezekiel must also eat and drink with trembling to portray Jerusalem’s coming fear and desolation. The Lord rejects the saying that prophetic visions fail or concern only a distant future. The days are near, and flattering predictions will cease. What God has spoken against the rebellious people will happen in their own days without further delay.

God condemns prophets who follow their own imaginations while claiming to speak for him. They have not strengthened Israel against danger but promise peace where there is none. Their assurances are compared to a badly plastered wall that a storm will expose and destroy. These prophets will lose their place among God’s people.

Ezekiel must also confront women who deceive and entrap people through their practices. For small payments they misrepresent God, discouraging the righteous and encouraging the wicked to continue in sin. The Lord promises to tear away the objects used in their deception and deliver his people from their hands. Their false visions and divinations will cease.

chapters.title: Idols in the heart and personal accountability

parts.text: When elders come to consult Ezekiel, God exposes the idols they have set up in their hearts. Their outward inquiry does not remove their inward estrangement. Israel is called to repent and turn from its abominations. Both deceptive prophets and those seeking them will bear responsibility, so that God’s people may cease wandering from him.

The Lord describes famine, wild beasts, sword, and pestilence as judgments upon a sinful land. Even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves by their righteousness, not their sons or daughters. Jerusalem will face all four judgments. A surviving remnant will come to the exiles, whose observation of their conduct will show that God’s judgment was not without cause.

The LORD asks Ezekiel what use vine wood has compared with the wood of other trees. It cannot provide timber for useful work or even a peg for hanging a vessel. Once fire has burned its ends and scorched its middle, it is less useful still.

God applies this picture to Jerusalem’s inhabitants. As vine wood is given to the fire, so they will be given over to judgment. Escaping one fire will not ensure safety from another. The Lord will set his face against them and make the land desolate because of their unfaithfulness. Through this judgment they will know that he is the LORD.

Jerusalem is portrayed as an abandoned infant whom God rescued, raised, and adorned. He entered into covenant with her, but she trusted her beauty and used his gifts for idolatry. The image becomes that of an unfaithful wife, seeking foreign lovers and even sacrificing her children. Instead of receiving payment, she pays others to join her unfaithfulness.

The Lord declares that her lovers will become her attackers, stripping and destroying her. Jerusalem’s sins surpass those of Samaria and Sodom; Sodom’s pride, abundance, neglect of the poor, and abominations are recalled. Yet judgment is not the final word. God promises restoration and an everlasting covenant, which will leave Jerusalem humbled and ashamed when he deals graciously with her.

chapters.title: The two eagles and the planted cedar

parts.text: Ezekiel tells a riddle about a great eagle taking the top of a cedar and planting seed that becomes a low spreading vine. The vine then turns toward another eagle for water, although its original planting supplied what it needed. God asks whether such a vine can prosper or withstand the drying east wind.

The explanation concerns Babylon’s king, the ruler he appointed in Jerusalem, and that ruler’s appeal to Egypt. Breaking the sworn covenant will bring captivity and defeat; Pharaoh cannot save him. God then promises to plant a tender cedar shoot on Israel’s high mountain. It will bear fruit and shelter birds, showing that he brings down the lofty and raises the lowly.

God rejects the proverb that children inevitably bear their fathers’ guilt. Every soul belongs to him, and the person who sins is accountable. Examples of a righteous father, a violent son, and a righteous grandson show that conduct is judged individually. The son who refuses his father’s wickedness will not die for that father’s iniquity.

The wicked person who turns from sin and does what is right will live, while the righteous person who abandons righteousness for evil cannot rely on past deeds. God answers accusations that his ways are unfair by exposing Israel’s own injustice. He calls the people to cast away their transgressions and make a new heart and spirit, declaring that he takes no pleasure in their death.

Ezekiel is told to lament for Israel’s princes. Their mother is pictured as a lioness raising cubs. One cub becomes a man-eating lion and is carried in chains to Egypt. Another becomes powerful and destructive, but the nations capture him and bring him to Babylon, ending his roar on Israel’s mountains.

The image changes to a fruitful vine planted beside water, with strong branches suitable for rulers’ scepters. In anger it is uprooted, dried by the east wind, and stripped of its strong branches. Now planted in a dry wilderness, it is consumed by fire coming from one of its own branches. No strong branch remains for a ruler’s scepter.

When elders seek guidance, God recounts Israel’s repeated rebellion. In Egypt, the wilderness, and the promised land, the people clung to idols, rejected his statutes, and profaned his sabbaths. Again and again he restrained destruction for his name’s sake before the nations. The present generation continues its fathers’ practices, including the sacrifice of children.

God declares that Israel will not simply become like the nations. He will gather the scattered people, judge them, and remove rebels before bringing them into their land. There they will serve him, remember their sins, and recognize his mercy toward his own name. A final message pictures an unquenchable fire consuming the southern forest; Ezekiel reports that people dismiss his words as parables.

The Lord commands Ezekiel to announce a drawn sword against Jerusalem and the land of Israel. The coming calamity will cut off righteous and wicked alike, leaving people trembling. Ezekiel must groan and strike his hands as he proclaims the sharpened, polished sword prepared for slaughter. No ruler’s authority can make the threat harmless.

The king of Babylon is pictured at a crossroads, using divination to choose between Jerusalem and the Ammonites. Jerusalem faces siege because its guilt has come to remembrance. Its wicked prince must lose his crown, and the rule will be overturned until the one whose right it is receives it. A separate warning declares that the Ammonites also face destruction despite deceptive assurances.

God exposes Jerusalem’s bloodshed, idolatry, oppression, sexual sins, and dishonest gain. Parents are dishonored, strangers and the vulnerable are mistreated, and holy things are despised. The city has forgotten the Lord and cannot withstand the day when he deals with it. Its inhabitants will be scattered among the nations.

Israel is compared to worthless metal gathered into a furnace; Jerusalem will become the place where God’s anger melts it. Prophets deceive, priests blur holy and unholy, rulers kill for profit, and ordinary people rob and oppress. God seeks someone to stand in the gap for the land but finds none. The judgment returns the people’s own conduct upon their heads.

Samaria and Jerusalem are portrayed as sisters named Aholah and Aholibah. Their unfaithfulness begins in Egypt and continues through their attraction to foreign powers and idols. Aholah seeks Assyria and is destroyed by her lovers. Aholibah sees her sister’s fate but becomes still more corrupt, turning toward Assyria, Babylon, and memories of Egypt.

God will turn Jerusalem’s former lovers against her, exposing and stripping her, destroying her children, and making her drink Samaria’s cup of desolation. Both sisters are charged with adultery, bloodshed, child sacrifice, and profaning God’s sanctuary and sabbaths. Their public judgment will reveal the consequence of their actions and teach others not to follow their practices.

chapters.title: The boiling pot and Ezekiel’s loss

parts.text: On the day Babylon begins besieging Jerusalem, God tells Ezekiel to record the date and speak a parable about a boiling pot. The pot represents the bloody city, whose uncleanness cannot be removed. Its contents are taken out, and the vessel itself is heated in the fire. Jerusalem’s refusal to be cleansed brings unavoidable judgment.

God tells Ezekiel that his wife will die and commands him to refrain from customary public mourning. After her death, his conduct becomes a sign to the people. They will lose the sanctuary they cherish and the children left in Jerusalem, yet waste away in their guilt without ordinary mourning. A survivor will bring the news, and Ezekiel’s mouth will be opened again.

God announces judgment on Ammon because it rejoiced over the desecration of his sanctuary, Israel’s desolation, and Judah’s captivity. Eastern peoples will possess its land, and its cities will become places for animals. Moab is also condemned for treating Judah as no different from the nations; its frontier cities will be opened to invaders.

Edom is charged with taking vengeance against Judah and will face devastation, with God’s vengeance carried out through Israel. The Philistines likewise acted from longstanding hatred and a desire to destroy. God declares that he will strike them and the remaining coastland inhabitants. Each announcement emphasizes that judgment will make the nations know that he is the LORD.

Tyrus celebrates Jerusalem’s ruin as an opportunity to increase its own prosperity. God answers that many nations will come against it like waves. Nebuchadrezzar and his army will besiege its walls, destroy its towers, and trample its streets. Its riches will be plundered, its buildings demolished, and its stones and timber cast into the water. Its songs will cease, and the place of its former splendor will become bare rock for spreading nets.

The seafaring rulers will leave their thrones, tremble, and lament the fall of the once-powerful maritime city. The islands will be shaken by news of its destruction. God portrays Tyrus as descending beneath the waters with those who go down into the pit.

A lament portrays Tyrus as a beautifully constructed ship, fitted with fine timber, embroidered sails, and skilled crews from many lands. Soldiers protect its walls, and a long list of trading partners shows its reach. Its markets exchange metals, livestock, food, fabrics, precious stones, spices, and even human beings, enriching rulers and peoples.

The splendid ship is then broken by an east wind in deep waters. Merchandise, sailors, craftsmen, merchants, and warriors fall together in its ruin. Mariners stand ashore in mourning, covering themselves with dust and sackcloth. Those enriched by its trade lament its destruction, while island inhabitants and kings are astonished. The image turns commercial greatness into a scene of overwhelming loss.

chapters.title: Pride brought down and Israel restored

parts.text: The prince of Tyrus claims divine standing because of his wealth and wisdom, but God declares him a man who will die at strangers’ hands. A lament over the king uses imagery of Eden, precious stones, and an anointed covering cherub. Beauty and privilege give way to pride, violence, and corruption; expulsion and destruction follow.

A separate oracle announces pestilence and bloodshed against Zidon, through which the Lord will display his holiness. Israel’s hostile neighbors will no longer be painful thorns. God promises to gather Israel from the nations into the land given to Jacob. They will build houses, plant vineyards, and dwell securely after he judges those around them who despised them.

chapters.title: Egypt humbled and given to Babylon

parts.text: Pharaoh is pictured as a great river creature claiming ownership of the river. God will draw him out with hooks and leave him exposed. Egypt has also proved a broken reed to Israel, injuring those who relied on it. The land will be desolate for forty years and its people scattered, then restored as a lowly kingdom. Egypt will cease to be Israel’s confidence.

A later message says Nebuchadrezzar’s army received no adequate reward for its exhausting service against Tyrus. God therefore gives Egypt to Babylon as payment for that labor, allowing its wealth and spoil to be taken. The Lord also promises renewed strength for Israel and an opened mouth for Ezekiel among his people.

Ezekiel announces a coming day of the Lord, a time of darkness and judgment for the nations. Egypt and its allies will fall together. Nebuchadrezzar’s army will devastate the land, and Egypt’s cities, idols, and sources of pride will be struck. The named cities face fire, sword, captivity, and fear, showing that none of Egypt’s centers can secure it.

In another dated message, God says Pharaoh’s arm is already broken and will not recover strength to hold a sword. He will break both arms and scatter the Egyptians. In contrast, he will strengthen Babylon’s king and place his own sword in that king’s hand. Egypt’s defeat will demonstrate that the Lord directs the judgment.

Pharaoh is asked to consider the Assyrian, pictured as a magnificent cedar nourished by abundant waters. Its height, beauty, and spreading branches surpass the other trees, and birds, animals, and nations find shelter beneath it. The imagery stresses the greatness of a kingdom whose resources and influence seemed secure.

Because the tree exalted itself, God delivered it to a powerful conqueror. Foreigners cut it down, its dependants abandoned it, and its fall shook the nations. The image follows the fallen tree into the world below, among those slain by the sword. This becomes a warning to every proud power and is explicitly applied to Pharaoh and his multitude: their greatness will not keep them from the same end.

Ezekiel laments Pharaoh, likening him to a lion and a sea creature troubling the waters. God will catch him in a net and leave him exposed as food for birds and beasts. Darkness will cover Egypt, other rulers will tremble, and Babylon’s sword will destroy its proud multitude. The nations are called to mourn its desolation.

A second lament portrays Egypt descending among the dead. Asshur, Elam, Meshech, Tubal, Edom, northern princes, and Zidonians are already there, their former terror replaced by shame. Pharaoh will join these defeated powers with his army, slain by the sword. The repeated picture removes the distinction between their earthly might and the common end that awaits them.

chapters.title: The watchman and news of Jerusalem

parts.text: The watchman’s trumpet illustrates Ezekiel’s responsibility to warn Israel. Those who ignore a warning bear their own guilt, but a silent watchman is accountable for failing them. God urges the wicked to turn and live, taking no pleasure in their death. Past righteousness cannot excuse present evil, and genuine repentance changes the wicked person’s course.

A survivor reports that Jerusalem has fallen; Ezekiel’s speech has already been restored before the messenger’s arrival. Those remaining in the land claim Abraham’s inheritance while continuing violence, idolatry, and adultery; God rejects their confidence. Among the exiles, people enjoy listening to Ezekiel but do not obey, treating him like a pleasing performer. When his warnings come true, they will recognize that a prophet was among them.

Israel’s shepherds are condemned for feeding themselves while neglecting the weak, injured, sick, and lost. Their harsh rule has scattered God’s flock and left it exposed to predators. The Lord will remove these shepherds and search for his sheep himself, bringing them from the nations to good pasture in their own land.

God also judges between members of the flock, confronting the strong who push aside the weak and spoil their food and water. He promises one shepherd, his servant David, and a covenant of peace. Harmful beasts, foreign oppression, hunger, and fear will give way to safety and fruitfulness. Israel will know that the Lord is with them and that they are his people.

God pronounces desolation on Mount Seir because of its enduring hatred toward Israel. It shed Israelite blood during their calamity and will itself be pursued by bloodshed. Its mountains and valleys will fill with the slain, and its cities will remain desolate. The judgment answers the violence in which it delighted.

Seir also claimed Israel and Judah’s territories as its own, despite the Lord’s presence there. God has heard its boasts against Israel’s mountains and against himself. He will repay its anger and envy. As Seir rejoiced when Israel’s inheritance was devastated, so it will experience devastation itself, while the Lord makes his identity and authority known.

chapters.title: A restored land and a new heart

parts.text: God speaks to Israel’s mountains, which enemies have mocked and claimed. The nations will bear their shame, while Israel’s land will again produce fruit and support a growing population. Ruined cities will be rebuilt. Israel’s earlier bloodshed and idolatry had brought exile, and its disgrace among the nations profaned the Lord’s name.

The Lord promises restoration for his holy name’s sake, not because Israel deserves it. He will gather the people, cleanse them, replace their stony heart, and put his Spirit within them so they obey him. They will inhabit their fathers’ land and remember their sins with shame. Fertile fields and rebuilt towns will show surrounding nations that the Lord restores what was desolate.

chapters.title: Dry bones and a reunited people

parts.text: Ezekiel sees a valley of dry bones. At God’s command he prophesies, and the bones join together, receive flesh, and finally live when breath enters them. God explains that the bones are the whole house of Israel, whose hope has failed. He promises to open their graves, bring them into their land, and put his Spirit within them.

Ezekiel joins two sticks representing Judah and Joseph. God explains that the scattered Israelites will become one nation under one king, no longer divided or defiled by idols. His servant David will be their shepherd and prince. God promises an everlasting covenant of peace and his sanctuary among them, so the nations will know that he sanctifies Israel.

God addresses Gog of Magog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and names a coalition of peoples with him. In the latter years they will come against Israel, gathered from the nations and dwelling safely. Gog plans to seize spoil from the restored land’s unwalled settlements, while merchants question the purpose of his invasion.

The vast army advances like a cloud, but God declares that the nations will know him through what follows. His anger brings a great shaking, collapsing mountains and walls. Gog’s forces turn their swords against one another and face pestilence, bloodshed, overflowing rain, hail, fire, and brimstone. The Lord magnifies his holiness before many nations through this judgment.

chapters.title: Gog’s defeat and the cleansing of the land

parts.text: God declares that Gog and his allies will fall on Israel’s mountains and become food for birds and beasts. Israel will burn their weapons for seven years and spend seven months burying the dead to cleanse the land. Workers will continue searching for remains, marking bones for burial in the valley named Hamon-gog.

Birds and beasts are summoned to God’s great sacrificial feast upon the defeated warriors. The nations will see his judgment and understand that Israel’s former captivity resulted from its own unfaithfulness. God promises mercy to the whole house of Israel, gathering the people from their enemies’ lands. He will no longer hide his face from them, having poured out his Spirit upon them.

In the twenty-fifth year of captivity, Ezekiel is brought in a vision to a high mountain in Israel. A man with measuring tools commands him to observe carefully and report what he sees. The outer wall, gates, guardrooms, porches, steps, windows, and pavement chambers are measured, with matching arrangements on the east, north, and south.

The guide measures the inner gates and courtyard, then shows facilities for washing and slaughtering sacrifices. Tables, instruments, and chambers are assigned to their purposes. Rooms are distinguished for priests serving the house and for the sons of Zadok who minister at the altar. The chapter ends with measurements of the temple porch and its pillars.

Ezekiel’s guide measures the temple entrance, main room, and inner sanctuary, identifying the inner square chamber as the most holy place. Measurements follow for the surrounding walls, three levels of side chambers, open spaces, and the building to the west. The description carefully distinguishes the temple itself from its adjoining structures.

The interior is paneled with wood and decorated with cherubims and palm trees. Each cherub has a human face toward one palm and a lion’s face toward another. A wooden altar is identified as the table before the LORD. Folding doors bear the same carved designs, while windows and porch details complete the account of the building’s furnishings and surfaces.

chapters.title: Holy chambers and the surrounding boundary

parts.text: The guide brings Ezekiel to chamber buildings beside the temple area. Their dimensions, entrances, galleries, and three stories are described, including matching arrangements on opposite sides. Upper rooms are narrower because of the galleries, and passageways connect the chambers with the courts.

These are holy rooms where priests eat and store the most holy offerings. Priests must leave their sacred service garments there and put on other clothing before entering areas used by the people. The guide then measures the outer boundary on all four sides, each five hundred reeds. Its wall separates the sanctuary from the common area beyond it.

chapters.title: God’s glory returns to the house

parts.text: Ezekiel sees the glory of Israel’s God approaching from the east, with a voice like many waters and brightness filling the earth. The glory enters the temple and fills it. God calls this the place of his throne and declares that Israel must no longer defile his name. Ezekiel must show the temple’s pattern and ordinances to the people so they are ashamed of their sins.

The altar’s dimensions, levels, horns, and steps are specified. Instructions follow for cleansing and consecrating it through sacrifices offered by the sons of Zadok. Seven days are appointed for this preparation. From the eighth day onward, burnt offerings and peace offerings will be presented, and God promises to accept the people.

The east gate remains shut because the Lord entered through it, though the prince has a designated place to eat before him. God forbids the former defilement of the sanctuary by uncircumcised strangers. Levites who led Israel into idolatry retain supporting duties but lose priestly access; the sons of Zadok, who remained faithful, may minister near him.

Regulations govern priestly clothing, hair, wine, marriage, and contact with the dead. Priests must distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean, teach the people, judge disputes, and keep God’s appointed observances. The Lord himself is their inheritance rather than a territorial possession. Offerings and firstfruits provide their food, subject to the restrictions of their sacred service.

chapters.title: Holy land, honest measures, and offerings

parts.text: A holy portion of land is set apart for the sanctuary and priests, with portions also assigned to Levites, the city, and the prince. Israel’s rulers must cease violence and dispossession, practice justice, and use honest weights and measures. The people’s contributions support offerings that the prince is responsible for providing at appointed occasions.

Instructions describe cleansing the sanctuary at the beginning of the year and providing for those who sin through error or ignorance. Passover and seven days of unleavened bread are observed in the first month, with specified sacrifices supplied by the prince for himself and the people. Corresponding offerings accompany the seven-day feast beginning in the seventh month.

The east gate of the inner court opens on sabbaths and new moons for worship. The prince and people have designated places and routes, and the prince supplies the appointed offerings. During festivals worshipers leave by the gate opposite their entrance. Voluntary offerings and the daily morning lamb are also regulated.

A prince may give inheritance to his sons, but grants to servants return at the year of liberty. He must not take the people’s property to provide for his own household. Ezekiel is then shown places where priests boil and bake holy offerings without carrying them into the public court, along with kitchens where ministers prepare the people’s sacrifices.

chapters.title: Life-giving waters and the land’s borders

parts.text: Water flows eastward from beneath the temple threshold. At measured distances it deepens from ankle height to a river too deep to cross. It heals the waters it reaches and supports abundant fish, though marshes remain salty. Trees along its banks bear fresh fruit continually, with fruit for food and leaves for medicine because their water comes from the sanctuary.

God sets the boundaries of the land to be inherited by Israel’s twelve tribes, with Joseph receiving two portions. The northern, eastern, southern, and western limits are described. Resident strangers who have children among the Israelites are to share the inheritance as native-born people. Their portion is assigned within the tribe where they live.

chapters.title: Tribal portions and the Lord’s city

parts.text: The land is arranged in portions for the tribes, beginning with Dan in the north and continuing through Judah. A central holy district includes the sanctuary, the priests’ and Levites’ land, and the city with its supporting farmland. The prince receives land on either side. The sacred portion cannot be sold or exchanged, and the city’s workers come from every tribe.

South of the central district are portions for Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun, and Gad. The city’s dimensions and twelve gates are then given, three on each side, named for Israel’s tribes. The vision closes with the city’s defining name: The LORD is there.
